The Battle of Goma

By: Graham Coetzer | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
With 14 dead and more than a hundred injured - the SANDF's withdrawal from the DRC was anything but covered in glory - now insiders paint a grim picture of a deployment gone horribly wrong.

Unique Selling Point:
SANDF soldiers who were caught up in the attack by M23 rebels earlier this year on South African bases in Sake and Goma want to speak out. They paint a grim picture of a deployment doomed to fail from the get go - inadequate operational plans, ill equipped bases and a failure of leadership during the battle are just some of their complaints. Serious questions raised around what happened to monies meant for the soldiers while on deployment have just added fuel to the fire. Now soldiers are willing to risk their careers to tell their stories.

Summary:
South African bases at Sake and Goma were overrun by M23 rebels earlier this year during the SANDF's SAMIDRC (South African Development Community Mission in the Democratic Republic of Congo.) 14 SANDF soldiers lost their lives, and a reported 174 were injured - some of them suffering life changing injuries.

Some of the soldiers who've returned are willing to speak to us on condition of anonymity. They site failures in planning, intelligence, logistics and leadership as the core issues behind South Africa's lack lustre performance against advancing M23 rebels.

A base commander was absent during the heat of the battle, soldiers were hung out to dry after they were caught outside the base when fighting started, and general mayhem ensued when the fighting reached fever pitch. Even after the fighting, when the SANDF had reportedly surrendered, the bases were a scene of chaos. Rations were in short supply, and some soldiers were forced to eat food from fridges that were storing the bodies of the dead. Basic medical kits were nowhere to be found.

On their return from the DRC after an equally disorganised withdrawal, the SANDF called their deployment in the DRC a success, but angry soldiers say they've had enough of the subterfuge and want to tell their stories.

Defense Union SANDU is claiming each member deployed be paid R8000 per day as well as a compensation amount of $1428 per soldier. This after claims that SADC allocated R108 000 per month per soldier over the period of deployment, while the troops only received R32 000 per month. Where the additional funds went remains a mystery.

Further information:
The soldiers willing to speak out were part of strategic units deployed to the DRC.
Because of fears of intimidation by the SANDF, the soldiers want to hide their identities.
We have soldiers from intelligence, artillery and other units.
One of our case studies was badly injured, losing both legs in the battle.

Battle Of Goma
FINAL Script
13 October 2025

(Govan) In the early hours of the 23rd of January this year, near the city of Goma in Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, a South African Defence Force base was jolted into life by a series of explosions and the sound of gunfire.

(Ups Cellphone Video Subtitles) Lay low lapa, lay low, lay low!

(Soldier 1 Subtitles) You know bombs are falling, everybody’s shooting, there’s chaos in the base.

(Govan) Months after an embarrassing withdrawal from a peace-keeping mission, the SANDF has allegedly tried to bury the events that unfolded in the days and weeks after that attack.

(Ricardo Teixeira) I can’t think of another instance when our troops were held captive by a non-state actor for about four months.

(Govan) Soldiers followed orders into chaos – now they’re breaking their silence.

(Soldier 2 Subtitles) It’s a betrayal of the men on the ground.

(Govan) The minister of defence claimed the mission provided an environment of safety, security and stability for the people of the City of Goma and surrounding areas, but for the troops on the ground, it was anything but.

(Govan) In 2023, our soldiers joined those from Tanzania and Malawi in a Southern African Development Community Mission known as SAMIDRC. Unlike traditional peacekeepers, they were deployed to actively combat rebel groups in the war-torn east of the DRC.

(Govan) Govan: Were we there to fight rebels?

(Ricardo Teixeira) We were there to fight rebels. We were there to fight a war. This was not a peacekeeping deployment. This was a deployment to conduct combat operations.

(Govan) The mission targeted M23, a Rwandan-backed rebel group long active in the DRC. South Africa helped neutralise them in 2013, and, according to defence analyst Ricardo Teixeira, this mission aimed to do the same.

(Ricardo Teixeira) If we look at what they went in with in 2013, you know they had Rooivalk attack helicopters, they had an air assault battalion, 6 SAI was contributed, they had special forces. But you also had attack helicopters that were contributed by the UN, you had a much larger force contingent.

(Ups Chopper)

(Govan) But that wasn’t the case this time around.

(Ricardo Teixeira) So they went into it this time thinking you know, this is just going to be like then. But they didn’t contribute the attack helicopters, there was not enough air cover for medical evacuation, the medical support on the ground was just not there.

(Govan) With little to no logistical and hardware support, 14 SANDF soldiers were killed and 174 reportedly injured in M23 attacks on SAMIDRC positions.

(Govan) Let’s do this.

(Govan) Many of those who fought frantically for survival feel betrayed by their superiors. And, for the first time, they’ve agreed to interviews.

(Soldier 2 Subtitles) Failure, failure, failure. Everything was just a failure. From the beginning, from the day I landed in Goma.

(Govan) This soldier suffered life-altering injuries during the battle in late January. He sensed something was wrong when he was sent to the front lines in an unarmed cargo truck.

(Soldier 2 Subtitles) Cargo trucks. No weapon, no ammunition. The enemy is on top there, they can spot us while we are coming.

(Govan) He was deployed to the South African base at Sake – a key outpost just 24 kilometers from Goma, and the launchpad for SAMIDRC’s combat operations. This soldier told us it was an area where M23 already held the high ground.

(Soldier 1 Subtitles) The initial plan was for South Africa to be on the mountain - as high ground. But the reality of the matter was, when we landed there, we ended up in a hole, so to say.

(Govan) But the poor strategic placement of our base wasn’t the only problem.

(Soldier 1 Subtitles) The majority bought our own tents - I bought my own tent as also, which cost me like R8000.

(Govan) Why?

(Soldier 1 Subtitles) Because there just wasn’t enough tents. They didn’t have tents. The basics of going we didn’t have.

(Govan) It speaks volumes about a mission undone not only by the enemy, but by poor logistics.

(Pikkie Greeff) Right from the start of the deployment, we had complaints from the ground saying our rations are not regular, our sleeping quarters, we have no sleeping quarters. We had to buy our own tents.

(Govan) Pikkie Greeff, from the South African National Defence Union, can’t hide his frustration at how the troops were let down by the military’s top brass.

(Pikkie Greeff) I would say it’s the most disastrous deployment that we’ve had post 1994…

(Govan) The January attacks followed months of skirmishes between our forces and M23 and began with sustained mortar fire on our base at Sake.

(Soldier 1 Subtitles) Bombs are falling, everybody’s shooting. There’s chaos in the base. Nobody knows what must happen.

(Govan) As the fighting raged, the chain of command appeared to collapse.

(Ricardo Teixeira) I know of several sergeants that had to take charge of companies because lieutenants, and captains and majors froze. With one major apparently at Sake going catatonic.

(Soldier 1 Subtitles) A lot of leaders were scared. Ja, a lot of leaders were scared.

(Govan) Worse still, M23 showed up with more men and bigger guns.

(Govan) Which moments do you remember?

(Soldier 2 Subtitles) The firepower of M23. It was too much.

(Soldier 1 Subtitles) They didn’t even ask questions; it was straight RPGs, LMGs, sniper rifles into the base. Even one sniper in battle - and you don’t have a sniper - it’s a game changer.

(Govan) Where was our sniper?

(Soldier 1 Subtitles) We didn’t have snipers.

(Govan) Why?

(Soldier 1 Subtitles) I don’t know what to say.

(Ricardo Teixeira) This was pretty intense, this was several thousand troops on each side, going at it. With again, artillery, there was brief support from UN MI-24 helicopters –

(Ups Chopper)

(Ricardo Teixeira) -and, you know, again, this was a proper fight.

(Govan) This footage shows SANDF troops firing Rocket Propelled Grenades, or RPG’s, at M23 positions. The fighting was intense, and soon Sake suffered its first casualties.


(Soldier 1 Subtitles) One of my friends was shot with a RPG. Another one died by a mortar. So, ja…

(Govan) The troops were sitting ducks, ordered to stay inside and not take the fight to M23.

(Govan) Can you remember the moment when the bomb hit?

(Soldier 2 Subtitles) Not really. I just saw myself lying down. There was a dark smoke. When I checked, I was injured.

(Govan) Caught in the explosion of a falling mortar round, he suffered injuries few could have survived.

(Soldier 2 Subtitles) I can’t describe that pain.

(Govan) Miraculously, the South African base at Sake was never overrun. But with our troops effectively pinned inside, M23 sent forces to Goma, the biggest town in the region and the site of a second SAMIDRC base.

(Soldier 1 Subtitles) The people in Goma were not a fighting element. They were not there to withstand a full-on attack.

(UPS FIGHTING)

(Govan) Two days after the attack on Sake started, M23 reached Goma.

(Ricardo Teixeira) You know once Sake was taken out, Goma was all that was left, and they went on in. It was about 7 days before it was all over in both cities.

(Govan) This widely shared video of a soldier raising a white flag in Goma summed up the humiliation of the SANDF at the hands of a rebel militia. But back in Sake, our troops were still fighting.

(Soldier 1 Subtitles) Our officer in charge called us at some point during the battle and said we are not fighting anymore. M23 has taken Goma town.

(Govan) How did you react to be told that?

(Soldier 1 Subtitles) I was in shock, I was speechless.

(Govan) The gunfire had stopped, but the danger hadn’t. Our troops were surrounded by M23 rebels. Running out of supplies, with no reinforcements in sight. They were stranded and exposed.

(Soldier 1 Subtitles) The soldiers were told that they must give up their weapons, by our own seniors. And M23 doesn’t want to see weapons in the base.

(Govan) So, once you handed your weapons back to the stores, what was the morale like?

(Soldier 1 Subtitles) It was like we surrendered. Like, how can we just give up our weapons? Okay we’re not fighting. But don’t ask me to give up my weapon. That is something on another level now.

(Soldier 1 Subtitles) Most of the SANDF wounded were taken to a public hospital in Goma without air support. A hospital surrounded by enemy forces.

(Govan) But you were a SANDF soldier in a public hospital, did you have protection there?

(Soldier 2 Subtitles) No, no protection. The hospital they said they will only provide us medical care -no food, nothing.

(Govan) In the weeks after the battle, food was a scarce commodity – and soldiers weren’t being paid their allowances.

(Soldier 1 Subtitles) I think we didn’t eat for nearly a week. The food ran out for like a week. We had to try and send a local to buy us some food. The conditions were just bad. There wasn’t food. We couldn’t get it in. And the amount of people versus the amount of people that must eat… It became something else.

(Govan) Where were you keeping the bodies in the base?

(Soldier 1 Subtitles) In the pantry where we held the food.

(Govan) What?

(Soldier 1 Subtitles) It’s what happened. We had to store our food in the pantry with the bodies. It’s a fact.

(Govan) Our troops were confined to base for months before being withdrawn from the DRC – not by air, but by bus through Rwanda and on to Tanzania, and then flown out on commercial airlines.

(Govan) A lot of analysts believe Rwanda backed the M23 rebels – was it humiliating to leave through Rwanda?

(Soldier 1 Subtitles) To say the least, yes. It’s like you are rubbing salt in our wounds.

(Soldier 2 Subtitles) All the injured members we were transported by bus. It was a rough day.

(Govan) Troops we spoke to knew the SAMIDRC mission would be dangerous, and they accepted that risk. But what they didn’t expect was to return home without the full pay they were promised. So where did that money go?

(Govan) Soldiers feel they were grossly underpaid for the DRC deployment.

(Soldier 1 Subtitles) Danger pay was I think R20.

(Govan) A day?

(Soldier 1 Subtitles) A day.

(Govan) The union is demanding R1500 per day – and sight of a memorandum of understanding signed between SADC and the South African government.

(Pikkie Greeff) We asked for the memorandum of understanding which was provided to us, but with very crucial annexures that shows you how the money should be allocated, they were not given to us. That’s being withheld from us.

(Govan) Which means they don’t know how money from SADC - meant to pay soldiers - was spent. And while the SANDF has not responded to our questions, distrust and defiance are brewing within the ranks.

(Ups Soldier 1 Subtitles) This is a cry for help for the people on the ground who are the ones doing the work. The ones who are injured, the ones who have been killed. Because you don’t see a general being killed in battle.

Show: Title Author Last Updated 19 October 2025 - Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 19 October 2025 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Script: Battle Of Goma FINAL Script 13 October 2025 (Govan) In the early hours of the 23rd of January this year, near the city of Goma in Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, a South African Defence Force base was jolted into life by a series of explosions and the sound of gunfire. (Ups Cellphone Video Subtitles) Lay low lapa, lay low, lay low! (Soldier 1 Subtitles) You know bombs are falling, everybody’s shooting, there’s chaos in the base. (Govan) Months after an embarrassing withdrawal from a peace-keeping mission, the SANDF has allegedly tried to bury the events that unfolded in the days and weeks after that attack. (Ricardo Teixeira) I can’t think of another instance when our troops were held captive by a non-state actor for about four months. (Govan) Soldiers followed orders into chaos – now they’re breaking their silence. (Soldier 2 Subtitles) It’s a betrayal of the men on the ground. (Govan) The minister of defence claimed the mission provided an environment of safety, security and stability for the people of the City of Goma and surrounding areas, but for the troops on the ground, it was anything but. (Govan) In 2023, our soldiers joined those from Tanzania and Malawi in a Southern African Development Community Mission known as SAMIDRC. Unlike traditional peacekeepers, they were deployed to actively combat rebel groups in the war-torn east of the DRC. (Govan) Govan: Were we there to fight rebels? (Ricardo Teixeira) We were there to fight rebels. We were there to fight a war. This was not a peacekeeping deployment. This was a deployment to conduct combat operations. (Govan) The mission targeted M23, a Rwandan-backed rebel group long active in the DRC. South Africa helped neutralise them in 2013, and, according to defence analyst Ricardo Teixeira, this mission aimed to do the same. (Ricardo Teixeira) If we look at what they went in with in 2013, you know they had Rooivalk attack helicopters, they had an air assault battalion, 6 SAI was contributed, they had special forces. But you also had attack helicopters that were contributed by the UN, you had a much larger force contingent. (Ups Chopper) (Govan) But that wasn’t the case this time around. (Ricardo Teixeira) So they went into it this time thinking you know, this is just going to be like then. But they didn’t contribute the attack helicopters, there was not enough air cover for medical evacuation, the medical support on the ground was just not there. (Govan) With little to no logistical and hardware support, 14 SANDF soldiers were killed and 174 reportedly injured in M23 attacks on SAMIDRC positions. (Govan) Let’s do this. (Govan) Many of those who fought frantically for survival feel betrayed by their superiors. And, for the first time, they’ve agreed to interviews. (Soldier 2 Subtitles) Failure, failure, failure. Everything was just a failure. From the beginning, from the day I landed in Goma. (Govan) This soldier suffered life-altering injuries during the battle in late January. He sensed something was wrong when he was sent to the front lines in an unarmed cargo truck. (Soldier 2 Subtitles) Cargo trucks. No weapon, no ammunition. The enemy is on top there, they can spot us while we are coming. (Govan) He was deployed to the South African base at Sake – a key outpost just 24 kilometers from Goma, and the launchpad for SAMIDRC’s combat operations. This soldier told us it was an area where M23 already held the high ground. (Soldier 1 Subtitles) The initial plan was for South Africa to be on the mountain - as high ground. But the reality of the matter was, when we landed there, we ended up in a hole, so to say. (Govan) But the poor strategic placement of our base wasn’t the only problem. (Soldier 1 Subtitles) The majority bought our own tents - I bought my own tent as also, which cost me like R8000. (Govan) Why? (Soldier 1 Subtitles) Because there just wasn’t enough tents. They didn’t have tents. The basics of going we didn’t have. (Govan) It speaks volumes about a mission undone not only by the enemy, but by poor logistics. (Pikkie Greeff) Right from the start of the deployment, we had complaints from the ground saying our rations are not regular, our sleeping quarters, we have no sleeping quarters. We had to buy our own tents. (Govan) Pikkie Greeff, from the South African National Defence Union, can’t hide his frustration at how the troops were let down by the military’s top brass. (Pikkie Greeff) I would say it’s the most disastrous deployment that we’ve had post 1994… (Govan) The January attacks followed months of skirmishes between our forces and M23 and began with sustained mortar fire on our base at Sake. (Soldier 1 Subtitles) Bombs are falling, everybody’s shooting. There’s chaos in the base. Nobody knows what must happen. (Govan) As the fighting raged, the chain of command appeared to collapse. (Ricardo Teixeira) I know of several sergeants that had to take charge of companies because lieutenants, and captains and majors froze. With one major apparently at Sake going catatonic. (Soldier 1 Subtitles) A lot of leaders were scared. Ja, a lot of leaders were scared. (Govan) Worse still, M23 showed up with more men and bigger guns. (Govan) Which moments do you remember? (Soldier 2 Subtitles) The firepower of M23. It was too much. (Soldier 1 Subtitles) They didn’t even ask questions; it was straight RPGs, LMGs, sniper rifles into the base. Even one sniper in battle - and you don’t have a sniper - it’s a game changer. (Govan) Where was our sniper? (Soldier 1 Subtitles) We didn’t have snipers. (Govan) Why? (Soldier 1 Subtitles) I don’t know what to say. (Ricardo Teixeira) This was pretty intense, this was several thousand troops on each side, going at it. With again, artillery, there was brief support from UN MI-24 helicopters – (Ups Chopper) (Ricardo Teixeira) -and, you know, again, this was a proper fight. (Govan) This footage shows SANDF troops firing Rocket Propelled Grenades, or RPG’s, at M23 positions. The fighting was intense, and soon Sake suffered its first casualties. (Soldier 1 Subtitles) One of my friends was shot with a RPG. Another one died by a mortar. So, ja… (Govan) The troops were sitting ducks, ordered to stay inside and not take the fight to M23. (Govan) Can you remember the moment when the bomb hit? (Soldier 2 Subtitles) Not really. I just saw myself lying down. There was a dark smoke. When I checked, I was injured. (Govan) Caught in the explosion of a falling mortar round, he suffered injuries few could have survived. (Soldier 2 Subtitles) I can’t describe that pain. (Govan) Miraculously, the South African base at Sake was never overrun. But with our troops effectively pinned inside, M23 sent forces to Goma, the biggest town in the region and the site of a second SAMIDRC base. (Soldier 1 Subtitles) The people in Goma were not a fighting element. They were not there to withstand a full-on attack. (UPS FIGHTING) (Govan) Two days after the attack on Sake started, M23 reached Goma. (Ricardo Teixeira) You know once Sake was taken out, Goma was all that was left, and they went on in. It was about 7 days before it was all over in both cities. (Govan) This widely shared video of a soldier raising a white flag in Goma summed up the humiliation of the SANDF at the hands of a rebel militia. But back in Sake, our troops were still fighting. (Soldier 1 Subtitles) Our officer in charge called us at some point during the battle and said we are not fighting anymore. M23 has taken Goma town. (Govan) How did you react to be told that? (Soldier 1 Subtitles) I was in shock, I was speechless. (Govan) The gunfire had stopped, but the danger hadn’t. Our troops were surrounded by M23 rebels. Running out of supplies, with no reinforcements in sight. They were stranded and exposed. (Soldier 1 Subtitles) The soldiers were told that they must give up their weapons, by our own seniors. And M23 doesn’t want to see weapons in the base. (Govan) So, once you handed your weapons back to the stores, what was the morale like? (Soldier 1 Subtitles) It was like we surrendered. Like, how can we just give up our weapons? Okay we’re not fighting. But don’t ask me to give up my weapon. That is something on another level now. (Soldier 1 Subtitles) Most of the SANDF wounded were taken to a public hospital in Goma without air support. A hospital surrounded by enemy forces. (Govan) But you were a SANDF soldier in a public hospital, did you have protection there? (Soldier 2 Subtitles) No, no protection. The hospital they said they will only provide us medical care -no food, nothing. (Govan) In the weeks after the battle, food was a scarce commodity – and soldiers weren’t being paid their allowances. (Soldier 1 Subtitles) I think we didn’t eat for nearly a week. The food ran out for like a week. We had to try and send a local to buy us some food. The conditions were just bad. There wasn’t food. We couldn’t get it in. And the amount of people versus the amount of people that must eat… It became something else. (Govan) Where were you keeping the bodies in the base? (Soldier 1 Subtitles) In the pantry where we held the food. (Govan) What? (Soldier 1 Subtitles) It’s what happened. We had to store our food in the pantry with the bodies. It’s a fact. (Govan) Our troops were confined to base for months before being withdrawn from the DRC – not by air, but by bus through Rwanda and on to Tanzania, and then flown out on commercial airlines. (Govan) A lot of analysts believe Rwanda backed the M23 rebels – was it humiliating to leave through Rwanda? (Soldier 1 Subtitles) To say the least, yes. It’s like you are rubbing salt in our wounds. (Soldier 2 Subtitles) All the injured members we were transported by bus. It was a rough day. (Govan) Troops we spoke to knew the SAMIDRC mission would be dangerous, and they accepted that risk. But what they didn’t expect was to return home without the full pay they were promised. So where did that money go? (Govan) Soldiers feel they were grossly underpaid for the DRC deployment. (Soldier 1 Subtitles) Danger pay was I think R20. (Govan) A day? (Soldier 1 Subtitles) A day. (Govan) The union is demanding R1500 per day – and sight of a memorandum of understanding signed between SADC and the South African government. (Pikkie Greeff) We asked for the memorandum of understanding which was provided to us, but with very crucial annexures that shows you how the money should be allocated, they were not given to us. That’s being withheld from us. (Govan) Which means they don’t know how money from SADC - meant to pay soldiers - was spent. And while the SANDF has not responded to our questions, distrust and defiance are brewing within the ranks. (Ups Soldier 1 Subtitles) This is a cry for help for the people on the ground who are the ones doing the work. The ones who are injured, the ones who have been killed. Because you don’t see a general being killed in battle.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): With 14 dead and more than a hundred injured - the SANDF's withdrawal from the DRC was anything but covered in glory - now insiders paint a grim picture of a deployment gone horribly wrong.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: SANDF soldiers who were caught up in the attack by M23 rebels earlier this year on South African bases in Sake and Goma want to speak out. They paint a grim picture of a deployment doomed to fail from the get go - inadequate operational plans, ill equipped bases and a failure of leadership during the battle are just some of their complaints. Serious questions raised around what happened to monies meant for the soldiers while on deployment have just added fuel to the fire. Now soldiers are willing to risk their careers to tell their stories.
metadata.Summary: South African bases at Sake and Goma were overrun by M23 rebels earlier this year during the SANDF's SAMIDRC (South African Development Community Mission in the Democratic Republic of Congo.) 14 SANDF soldiers lost their lives, and a reported 174 were injured - some of them suffering life changing injuries. Some of the soldiers who've returned are willing to speak to us on condition of anonymity. They site failures in planning, intelligence, logistics and leadership as the core issues behind South Africa's lack lustre performance against advancing M23 rebels. A base commander was absent during the heat of the battle, soldiers were hung out to dry after they were caught outside the base when fighting started, and general mayhem ensued when the fighting reached fever pitch. Even after the fighting, when the SANDF had reportedly surrendered, the bases were a scene of chaos. Rations were in short supply, and some soldiers were forced to eat food from fridges that were storing the bodies of the dead. Basic medical kits were nowhere to be found. On their return from the DRC after an equally disorganised withdrawal, the SANDF called their deployment in the DRC a success, but angry soldiers say they've had enough of the subterfuge and want to tell their stories. Defense Union SANDU is claiming each member deployed be paid R8000 per day as well as a compensation amount of $1428 per soldier. This after claims that SADC allocated R108 000 per month per soldier over the period of deployment, while the troops only received R32 000 per month. Where the additional funds went remains a mystery.
metadata.Further information: The soldiers willing to speak out were part of strategic units deployed to the DRC. Because of fears of intimidation by the SANDF, the soldiers want to hide their identities. We have soldiers from intelligence, artillery and other units. One of our case studies was badly injured, losing both legs in the battle.
